extra.message: Missing authentication on message creation API endpoint — Unauthenticated attackers can inject stored XSS payloads, spam the message system, or impersonate arbitrary users via the from_user field. [verified: MessagesView.post() at api/views.py:43 has no @admin_required or @login_required decorator, unlike all other methods in the same class (index, get, delete, acknowledge_message). No blueprint-level or app-level before_request middleware enforces auth on /api/v1/ routes. The stored message fields (message, from_user) are rendered with Jinja2 |safe filter in admin/message.html, enabling unauthenticat]

Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY enables session forgery — Attacker forges signed session cookies to impersonate any user including admin, bypassing all authentication. [verified: SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as a static string at line 23 in config_app() with no environment variable or config file override; anyone who knows the key can forge valid Flask signed session cookies for any user including admin.]

DEBUG=True enabled with interactive debugger in production — Attackers can trigger exceptions to access the Werkzeug debugger console, execute arbitrary Python code on the server, and read sensitive configuration and source code. [verified: DEBUG is unconditionally set to True at line 26 with no environment check; unhandled exceptions expose the Werkzeug interactive debugger allowing arbitrary Python code execution and source code disclosure.]

DEBUG mode enabled in production — Attackers triggering errors can access interactive Python shell on the server, read source code, environment variables, and database contents via the Werkzeug debugger. [verified: DEBUG is unconditionally set to True at line 26 with no environment check; unhandled exceptions expose the Werkzeug interactive debugger allowing arbitrary Python code execution and source code disclosure.]

Plaintext password storage — All user passwords exposed on database breach; credentials reused across services are compromised. [verified: User model stores passwords as plaintext via db.Column(db.String(200)) at models.py:11 with direct assignment in __init__ at line 14, and login/views.py:17 compares user.password == password with zero hashing — a database compromise exposes all credentials.]

Plaintext password storage — Any database compromise (e.g. SQLite file theft, backup exposure, or admin panel access) reveals all user passwords in cleartext, enabling credential reuse attacks and full account compromise. [verified: Same plaintext storage as finding [0]: no hashing, no salting, direct plaintext comparison at login/views.py:17, and the password column is a bare String field at models.py:11.]

Hardcoded default admin credentials — Unauthenticated attacker gains admin access by simply logging in with admin/admin, granting full access to the admin panel, user data, message management, and API endpoints. [verified: The login template at app/blueprints/login/templates/login/login.html publicly displays 'Use credentials admin/admin to log in as admin', the add_admin CLI command in manage.py:14 defaults password='admin', and is_admin in models.py:20 is purely username=='admin' with no forced password change, allowing any visitor to gain full admin access with known credentials.]

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) on all state-changing forms — An attacker can trick an authenticated victim into visiting a malicious page that silently changes the victim's password, email, or submits feedback/API actions on their behalf, leading to full account takeover. [verified: No CSRF protection exists anywhere: zero 'csrf' references in the entire codebase, no Flask-WTF/WTForms in requirements.txt, no csrf_token in any form template (verified in forms.html macro and account_area.html), and no CSRF middleware or decorator on any state-changing POST endpoint including /account_area/change_password, /account_area/change_email, /login, and all API routes—enabling full acco]

Message sender spoofing via from_user parameter — An attacker can craft messages that appear to come from the admin or other trusted users, enabling social-engineering attacks against admins viewing the messages panel. [verified: from_user is accepted directly from the JSON request body (data.get('from_user','Anonymous')) at api/views.py:50 with no validation against current_user identity. Combined with the missing authentication on post(), an attacker can set from_user to 'admin' or any arbitrary username, and the value is rendered with |safe in the admin panel, enabling impersonation and social engineering.]

Missing CSRF protection on all state-changing endpoints — Attacker can forge cross-site requests to change victim's password, email, inject feedback, or perform actions authenticated as the victim. [verified: Flask-WTF is not installed (absent from requirements.txt) and no csrf_token appears in any template or view; all state-changing endpoints (login, change_password, change_email, send_feedback) lack CSRF tokens with no alternative origin-validation control present anywhere in the codebase.]

No rate limiting on login endpoint enables brute-force — Attacker brute-forces user credentials; combined with known admin username and weak default password, admin account takeover is trivial. [verified: No Flask-Limiter or any rate-limiting library is installed (confirmed in requirements.txt), no rate-limit decorator/middleware/account-lockout/CAPTCHA exists anywhere in the codebase, and the /auth/login endpoint at login/views.py:9-22 accepts unlimited POST guesses against plaintext passwords with a publicly-displayed admin username.]

Missing Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Protection on All State-Changing Forms — Attacker can force authenticated users to change their password, email, send feedback, or perform logout actions without their knowledge by tricking them into visiting a malicious page. [verified: Identical CSRF finding — all state-changing POST forms (login/views.py:10, account_area/views.py:16/44/62) lack CSRF tokens, Flask-WTF is uninstalled, and no server-side origin or referer validation compensates; attacker can forge cross-site requests to hijack victim sessions.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoint — Unrestricted brute-force password guessing against user accounts, enabling automated account takeover [verified: Same login endpoint at login/views.py:12 — no rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or any brute-force protection exists anywhere in the app; the admin username is displayed on the login page and passwords are stored in plaintext, enabling unrestricted automated password guessing.]

Session cookies missing Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite flags — Session cookies can be stolen via MITM on HTTP connections or via XSS (HttpOnly missing), enabling session hijacking. [verified: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is not set (defaults False in Flask 0.12.2) so session cookies transmit over unencrypted HTTP enabling MITM hijacking; SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY defaults to True so that flag is present, but the missing Secure flag alone is sufficient for exploitation.]

Plaintext passwords exposed in API responses via User.serialize — All user plaintext passwords are returned in API responses to admin users, creating a mass credential exposure risk if the API is compromised, logged, or intercepted. [verified: User.serialize includes self.password (models.py:32) and UsersView.index() calls .serialize on all users (api/views.py:72), returning plaintext passwords in JSON responses to any admin — a genuine information exposure even behind admin_required.]

Open redirect via ?next= parameter — Attacker uses the app's redirect to phish credentials or deliver malware by making the redirect appear to originate from the trusted domain. [verified: Attacker-controlled request.args.get('next') flows directly into Flask's redirect() at line 12 with zero validation — no is_safe_url check, no decorator, no middleware, no ALLOWED_HOSTS restriction exists anywhere in the codebase.]

X-XSS-Protection disabled by default with no CSP — Browser XSS filter is disabled globally, removing a fallback defense against reflected XSS attacks; no CSP means injected scripts execute with no restrictions. [verified: The after_request handler at line 73 sets X-XSS-Protection: 0 by default and no Content-Security-Policy header is configured anywhere; CSP absence removes a meaningful restriction on injected script execution, though X-XSS-Protection is a deprecated defense-in-depth control.]

Plaintext passwords and form data logged to console via print(request.form) — User credentials including plaintext passwords are written to server logs/console output where they can be read by anyone with log access, compromising all users whose password changes or feedback submissions are logged. [verified: Line 65's print(request.form) unconditionally writes all form fields submitted to /account_area/send_feedback to stdout/server logs, which is a reachable authenticated endpoint. However, the finding's claim that change_password form passwords are logged is incorrect — change_password() is a separate route handler with no print() call; only the feedback field (textarea 'feedback') is normally submi]

Missing CSRF protection on logout endpoint — Attacker can force-logout authenticated users by tricking them into loading a malicious page or link, causing denial of service and potentially facilitating social engineering or session-related attacks. [verified: The logout endpoint accepts GET (methods=['POST','GET']) and calls logout_user() with zero CSRF protection; no csrf_token fields exist in any template, and no CSRF middleware or validation is configured anywhere in the codebase. An attacker can embed a simple to force-logout authenticated victims.]
